newsitem.title: USA: AT&T charts new course in stormy waters.
newsitem.headline: AT&T charts new course in stormy waters.

text.p: AT&T Corp. this week promised its biggest critics that it will provide what customers want, overtake a legion of competitors, and finally make some money for its long-suffering shareholders.

But Wall Street showed its doubts about the five-year earnings target set by AT&T Chief Operating Officer John Walter, and its fright at the cost of achieving it by knocking 10 percent off the company's already depressed shares.
"AT&T faces the biggest challenge of its existence to execute this plan," said consultant Jeffrey Kagan of Kagan Telecom.

Walter, in his first presentation to Wall Street analysts, set a mouth-watering earnings target of $5 to $6 per share for the year 2001. That compares with the $3.47 per share, or $5.61 billion, the company earned in 1996.
"I'm confident we can reach that target," said Walter, who is slated to take over as chairman and chief executive from Robert Allen in 1998.
But analysts are not so sure, and were shocked by the billions AT&T plans to invest to get there.
Walter warned that the cost of building an AT&T that can compete across all services will squeeze 1997 profits year to between $2.45 and $3, down from the $3.47 made in 1996.
AT&T's stock closed Tuesday at $36, down 87.5 cents on the day, and $3.875, or 10 percent, since Monday's announcement.

For AT&T shareholders five years is a long time to wait. They have seen their shares drop more than 30 percent in the last year, adjusted for the spin-off of telecommunications equipment maker Lucent Technologies Inc.
"The five year forecast is a stretch. Investors are going to view this as a wait-and-see situation," said Merrill Lynch analyst Daniel Reingold.
Walter said that AT&T would invest $8 billion to $9 billion this year -- a big jump from the $6.8 billion spent in 1996, and this would hurt earnings.
Most of the money will be spent on new networks to handle high speed data, and on expanding wireless services.
Ironically, part of the problem is none other than Lucent, which was spun off by AT&T in September and is now charging its former parent full price for supplies.
Walter said that AT&T would cut $2.6 billion from costs in just two years, without increasing job cuts from the 11,200 already planned by the end of 1998.

He aims to speed management decision making, and is already reorganizing the sales force so a customer can get most of what they need from one sales representative, instead of having to deal with a host of product-based specialists.
Analysts approve of Walter's shirt-sleeve management style, in contrast to the aloof style of Robert Allen, and like his determination to make AT&T faster to market and more responsive to customers.
But they say the markets which are coalescing because of the 1996 Telecommunications Act will not stand still while AT&T enters local calling markets and expands its wireless service.
"This is a time of very dynamic change in the industry. Yesterday's leaders are not guaranteed to be tomorrow's leaders," said Kagan.

AT&T's traditional arch enemies like Sprint Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. now have big, wealthy foreign allies, while firms like WorldCom Inc. are touting advanced networks wholesale to small aggressive resellers to allow them to offer bundles of telecom services.
AT&T, with almost 60 percent of the $80 billion long distance market, is directly in the line of fire of the regional Bells as they enter the long distance market in force later this year.
GTE Corp., a local phone company which already offers long distance service, has shown how dangerous the Bells could be. It has already won a million long distance customers in one year.
"John Walter's actions are of a leader that people want to follow, but we need to know where we are going," said David Goodtree, an analyst at Forrester Research.
